summary: Epsilon Indi B is a pair of brown dwarfs, objects too small to shine by fusing hydrogen, orbiting the star Epsilon Indi 12.1 light-years away. WANDERERS saw it move 76 arcseconds from 2010 to 2026, or 4.70 arcseconds per year, which matches Gaia's 4.68. It is 2.7 times brighter at 4 to 4.75 microns than at 3.3 microns, where methane in cold atmospheres absorbs light. Its brightness stayed steady within the 0.03 magnitude uncertainty. Confidence is high, though 91 of 249 spectrum points were flagged.

qa.q: Why do we think this is what the card says?
qa.a: It moved 76 arcseconds between 2010 and 2026, or 4.70″ per year. That is within 0.3% of the speed Gaia DR3 lists for this source, which is about 12.1 light-years away. It is also 2.7 times brighter at 4–4.75 µm than in the 3.3 µm band, where methane absorbs light. A normal star would be below 1, but a cold brown dwarf comes out well above it. One caution: 91 of 249 spectrum points are flagged.

qa.q: What would make you less sure?
qa.a: Ninety-one of the 249 spectrum points are flagged, so parts of the spectrum are uncertain. This is a pair of brown dwarfs, and SPHEREx's large pixels likely blend both into one spot. Light from the bright star Epsilon Indi could also leak in. The brightness test can only rule out changes bigger than about 0.03 magnitudes. If later visits showed the methane dip fading, I'd worry.

qa.q: Why use both WISE and SPHEREx?
qa.a: WISE photographed this patch of sky in 2010, so it gives the starting point. SPHEREx imaged it again in 2025–2026. Over that 16-year gap, Epsilon Indi B moved 76 arcseconds, about 12 SPHEREx pixels. That was enough to measure its speed: 4.70 arcseconds per year, against Gaia's 4.68. SPHEREx also splits light into many colors. It caught the methane dip of a cold brown dwarf: 2.7 times brighter at 4–4.75 microns than at 3.3.
